extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, actors, and theatre practitioners/critics (English stage)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and staging tragedies for the English theatre: how to move terror and pity by writing and stagecraft, what stage-actions to represent or relate, and how to avoid cheap spectacle that undermines dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Move audience by sentiments and expressions, not dresses and decorations
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary Writers in Tragedy endeavour to raise Terror and Pity ... not by proper Sentiments and Expressions, but by the Dresses and Decorations of the Stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer raising emotion through dignified thought and sublime expression rather than relying on costume, set-dressings, thunder, or other outward trappings. The author criticises English practice of using visual adornment to manufacture feeling; understanding readers/audiences see through such artifices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making a hero by costume (plumes, trains, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary Method of making an Hero, is to clap a huge Plume of Feathers upon his Head ... One would believe that we thought a great Man and a tall Man the same thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't use exaggerated head-dresses, sweeping trains, or similar ornaments to signify greatness — these impede acting (awkward neck posture, page attending train) and distract the audience from the spoken dignity. Grandeur should come from thought and speech, not accoutrement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dignity of thought and sublimity of expression over trappings
rubrics_metrics.description: I would have our Conceptions raised by the Dignity of Thought and Sublimity of Expression, rather than by a Train of Robes or a Plume of Feathers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft lines and sentiments that generate majestic ideas in the audience; good language and thought will convey heroism and majesty far better than costly visual artifices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not represent large-scale incidents (armies/battles) onstage; narrate them
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible for the Reader's Imagination to multiply twenty Men into such prodigious Multitudes ... Incidents of such a Nature should be told, not represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid staging vast armies or battles in small theatres; use narration or description to allow the audience's imagination to supply grandeur. Practical staging limits make verbal depiction more effective and believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave guards and noisy martial pageantry offstage
rubrics_metrics.description: I should therefore ... recommend the Example of the French Stage, where the Kings and Queens always appear unattended, and leave their Guards behind the Scenes. I should likewise be glad if we imitated the French in banishing from our Stage the Noise of Drums, Trumpets, and Huzzas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from filling the stage with halberds, drums, trumpets and pseudo-armies to create dignity; such noise and show often overwhelm the text and are better implied or kept offstage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use stage effects (thunder, lightning, bells, ghosts) only with skill and proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be a proper Season for these several Terrors; and when they only come in as Aids and Assistances to the Poet, they are not only to be excused, but to be applauded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage machinery (thunder, lightning, bells, ghosts) can be effective when introduced with restraint and accompanied by suitable writing and preparation (examples: the clock in 'Venice Preserved', the Ghost in 'Hamlet'). Do not deploy effects merely as crude tricks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare the audience for supernatural appearances (ghosts) via preceding discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mind of the Reader is wonderfully prepared for his Reception by the Discourses that precede it: His Dumb Behaviour at his first Entrance, strikes the Imagination very strongly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A ghost or spectre is most terrifying when the play's dialogue and earlier scenes condition the audience; make sure preceding exposition and tone support the apparition so its appearance has literary force rather than being a cheap surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the handkerchief (or pity-instruments) judiciously; align speech with gesture
rubrics_metrics.description: For the moving of Pity, our principal Machine is the Handkerchief ... All that I would contend for, is, to keep it from being misapplied. In a Word, I would have the Actor's Tongue sympathize with his Eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Props used to elicit pity (handkerchiefs, children, etc.) should be integrated with appropriate speech and characterization. Avoid mechanical or incongruent uses that signal sentimentality rather than genuine emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid multiplying pathetic objects to manufacture pity (overuse becomes ridiculous)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Modern Writer ... brought a Princess upon the Stage with a little Boy in one Hand and a Girl in the other ... a third Poet ... introduced three Children, with great Success. Thus several Incidents that are beautiful in a good Writer, become ridiculous by falling into the Hands of a bad one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using children or multiplying tragic tokens to crank up audience sympathy can work once; repeated or excessive use turns into farce. Let pity arise from honest character and situation, not accumulation of contrived props.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid representing murders and bloody deeds onstage; prefer offstage execution and report
rubrics_metrics.description: There is none so absurd and barbarous ... as that dreadful butchering of one another, which is so very frequent upon the English Stage. Murders and Executions are always transacted behind the Scenes in the French Theatre ... the Fact ought not to have been represented, but to have been told, if there was any Occasion for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graphic depictions of killing onstage are indecent and appeal to a cruel curiosity; execute such acts offstage and use cries, reported dialogue, or aftermath to preserve dignity and increase emotional effect (example: Sophocles' handling of Orestes).

rubrics_metrics.name: When an action is improper for the scene, relate it rather than stage it
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Non tamen intus Digna geri promes in scenam: multaque tolles Ex oculis, qua mox narret facundia proesens.' Yet there are things improper for a Scene, Which Men of Judgment only will relate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect limits of decorum: certain events (extreme indecency, monstrous deeds, huge spectacles) should be narrated, not enacted, to maintain audience sensibility and poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary that scenery and wardrobe ('Tailor and Painter') often trump the poet for ordinary audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tailor and the Painter often contribute to the Success of a Tragedy more than the Poet. Scenes affect ordinary Minds as much as Speeches; and our Actors are very sensible, that a well-dressed Play has sometimes brought them as full Audiences, as a well-written one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that spectacle can secure box-office success among less discerning spectators, but balancing visual appeal with strong writing is necessary; relying solely on show risks contempt from more understanding viewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'Fourberia della Scena' — trickish stage knavery to impose upon spectators
rubrics_metrics.description: The Italians have a very good Phrase to express this Art of imposing upon the Spectators by Appearances: They call it the Fourberia della Scena, The Knavery or trickish Part of the Drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject cheap theatrical trickery intended to deceive or awe the audience with mere illusion. Strive for truthful dramatic means rather than contrivances that cheat the spectator's sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't darken the stage or use mechanical effects as substitutes for melancholy or terror
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Author has a mind to terrify us, it thunders; When he would make us melancholy, the Stage is darkened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the mechanical habit of altering lights/sounds as a lazy substitute for thoughtful writing that evokes mood. Use such effects sparingly and only when they complement well-crafted sentiments and expression.
